title: Private Deployments: VPC & On‑Prem Deployment Reference, Packaging, Day‑2 Ops, Upgrade & Rollback, and Customer Requirements
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary:

This document is a consolidated reference for Redwood Inference private deployments. It covers recommended VPC and on‑prem reference architectures, packaging and installation notes for on‑prem customers, a consolidated customer requirements library, and detailed day‑2 operational guidance including upgrade and rollback procedures. The intended audience is engineering, solutions, and customer operations teams who run, deploy, or support private Redwood clusters.

Scope and goals:
- Provide a single authoritative read‑me for deployment preconditions and expectations.
- Standardize upgrade and rollback procedures to minimize downtime and data risk.
- Define day‑2 operational runbooks (monitoring, scaling, backups, incident response).
- Capture customer requirements commonly requested during presales and legal review.

1) High‑level reference architectures

1.1 VPC deployment (recommended for cloud private):
- Topology: Customer VPC with private subnets for inference nodes, a management subnet for the control plane, and optional public subnet for egress/bastion.
- Components and ownership:
  - Customer managed VPC: networking, NAT gateways, transit gateway (if multi‑region).
  - Redwood Private control plane (optional customer‑managed or Redwood‑managed endpoint): API endpoints, web console access, audit log ingestion.
  - Inference nodes: GPU nodes in private subnets, autoscaling group or managed node pool.
  - Data plane: S3‑compatible object store for model artifacts (customer or cloud provider), persistent volumes for KV caches and metadata (if required).
- Network patterns and routing:
  - All inference traffic stays within private subnets; egress limited to required endpoints (container registries, Redwood control plane).
  - Use AWS PrivateLink/Interface endpoints for control plane access where available.

1.2 On‑prem (air‑gapped / co‑located) reference architecture:
- Topology: Rack or cluster hosting for GPU servers, separate management network for orchestration, optional DMZ for remote access (bastion).
- Components and ownership:
  - Customer provided hardware: GPU servers (NVIDIA A100/H100 recommended), top‑of‑rack switches, storage array for model artifacts/weights.
  - Redwood on‑prem package: container images, runtime binary, service manifests (Helm/Kustomize) and tooling for installation.
  - Optional private control plane (customer runs control plane inside their cluster) for fully air‑gapped setups.
- Key constraints:
  - Time sync (NTP) across nodes required.
  - Local image registry strongly recommended for air‑gapped installs.

2) Packaging & installation (on‑prem packaging notes)

2.1 Distribution artifacts
- Delivered artifacts:
  - Signed container images (tar archives for air‑gapped imports).
  - Helm charts and Kustomize overlays for supported Kubernetes distributions.
  - Installer CLI (redwoodctl) for validated install/upgrade workflows.
  - SHA256 checksums and GPG signatures for all artifacts.

2.2 Installation prechecks (example checklist):
- Minimum hardware:
  - GPU nodes: 4 x A100 80GB (baseline), or equivalent; refer to quantitative capacity planning for model‑specific recommendations.
  - Management node: 4 vCPU / 16GB RAM for control plane components.
  - Storage: 10TB NVMe or networked storage depending on model catalog size.
- Network:
  - Private management network with DNS resolving internal hostnames.
  - Firewall rules permitting required ports (see network & security section).
- Software:
  - Kubernetes 1.24–1.27 (certified distributions documented in release notes).
  - Container runtime: containerd 1.6+ or Docker 20.10+.
  - Node driver and GPU plugins installed (NVIDIA driver + CUDA + NVIDIA device plugin).

2.3 Example installer invocation (managed/connected install):
- redwoodctl install --profile onprem --manifest ./release/2027.02.10/manifest.yaml --registry my-registry.internal:5000 --accept-terms

2.4 Typical on‑prem install files
- Sample Kustomize overlay (snippets):
  apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
  kind: Kustomization
  resources:
    - ../../base
  images:
    - name: registry.redwood.internal/runtime
      newName: my-registry.internal/runtime
      newTag: 2027.02.10

3) Customer requirements library (consolidated)

This section lists common commercial, security, and technical requirements Redwood collects during presales and professional services engagements. Use as a checklist when sizing proposals and legal/security reviews.

Table: common customer requirements (pipe separated for readability)
| Requirement | Typical ask | Redwood recommendation / notes | Owner |
|------------|-------------|-------------------------------|-------|
| Data residency | Customer requires models & logs remain in region X | Deploy control plane and inference nodes in customer region; restrict egress. | Solutions Eng |
| Audit logging retention | 7+ years of audit logs | Provide log export to customer-managed S3 or on‑prem storage; redact PII in transit. | Security Team |
| Key management | Bring your own key (KMS/HSM) | Support customer KMS for model artifact encryption and TLS certs. | Security |
| Airgap support | No outbound internet allowed | Provide artifact tarball + internal registry instructions and offline activation key. | Professional Services |
| SLA / availability | 99.9% monthly | Dedicated capacity options with SLA contract; recommend multi‑AZ or redundant racks. | Sales / SRE |
| Vulnerability scanning | Regular container and OS scans | Provide SBOMs and image signatures; support scheduled vuln scans in customer environment. | Security |

4) Network & security: ports, firewall rules, and identity

4.1 Minimum network ports (example)
- Internal control plane <-> inference nodes: TCP 8443 (gRPC/HTTPS), 9090 (metrics), 2222 (administrative shell if enabled).
- Artifact store: HTTPS 443 (or S3 API endpoint port), registry port 5000 for local registries.
- Monitoring & logging: Prometheus scrape port 9100 (node exporter), Loki ingestion ports (3100).
- Health checks: Liveness/readiness via standard K8s probes (HTTP 8080).

4.2 Firewall examples (AWS Security Group snippets):
- Inference nodes SG:
  - Allow inbound 8443 from control-plane-subnet CIDR
  - Allow NTP from management NTP server
  - Deny all inbound from public internet

4.3 Identity and access
- Recommend customer uses SSO for console access (SAML/OIDC).
- Control plane service accounts should have least privilege for model artifact access.
- Use short‑lived certificates (automated rotation) and log key rotation events.

5) Day‑2 operations (monitoring, backups, scaling, incident response)

5.1 Observability and dashboards
- Baseline dashboards shipped with install:
  - Per‑node GPU utilization (GPU mem, GPU util, temperature).
  - Per‑model latency and token/sec throughput.
  - Cache hit ratio and KV cache sizes.
  - Error rates and 5xx breakdowns by route/model.
- Alerts and SLOs:
  - SLO: 99% requests <= 300ms tail latency (configurable per customer).
  - Alert: node GPU memory > 90% for 5m -> paging SRE oncall.
  - Alert: model load failure rate > 1% for 10m -> trigger automated rollback to previous model.

5.2 Backups and persistence
- Metadata store: daily snapshots of metadata DB (cronbackup to customer S3).
- Model artifacts: immutable object store; keep versioned model objects with lifecycle policy.
- KV caches: ephemeral; if using persistent cache, run consistent snapshot job before upgrades.

5.3 Scaling and capacity
- Horizontal scaling: node pool autoscaler based on per‑node token/sec thresholds.
- Vertical scaling: guidance for increasing GPU type/size per model.
- Capacity planning checklist:
  - Peak concurrent requests
  - Average sequence length distribution
  - Target p50/p95 latency
  - Cost constraints (preferred fallbacks to quantized variants)

5.4 Routine maintenance operations
- Log rotation: retain 90 days by default, export older logs to customer archive.
- Security patches: quarterly OS/driver patch window recommended with canary nodes.
- Game day exercises: quarterly simulated failover test to validate redundancy.

6) Upgrade and rollback procedures (detailed)

6.1 Principles
- Always stage upgrades in a non‑prod mirror of customer environment first.
- Use canary rollouts by percentage of traffic; validate latency and error budgets before promoting.
- Maintain immutable model artifact versions and changelogs.
- Keep at least two successful previous releases available for rollback.

6.2 Typical upgrade flow (control plane and runtime):
1. Prepare:
   - Run preupgrade checks (disk space, DB backups, image availability).
   - Snapshot metadata DB and export to secure storage.
   - Ensure model artifacts are present and checksums verified.
2. Canary rollout:
   - Deploy new control plane to canary namespace or canary replicas (10% traffic).
   - Deploy new runtime to a small subset of inference nodes (1-2 nodes).
   - Run synthetic traffic tests from traffic generator: correctness, latency, throughput.
3. Validation gates (automated):
   - Latency regression: p95 increase > 10% -> fail gate.
   - Error rate: new 5xx > 0.5% absolute increase -> fail gate.
   - Model output quality: run a small eval prompt set; significant regressions -> fail.
4. Progressive promotion:
   - If canary passes, promote to 50% then 100% using rolling upgrade strategy (cordon/drain patterns for K8s).
5. Postupgrade verification:
   - Confirm metrics & logs for 24h, run smoke tests, and collect customer signoff for major releases.

6.3 Rollback decision tree and actions:
- Trigger conditions for rollback:
  - Canary gate failure, sustained latency regressions, or critical errors affecting >1% of requests.
- Immediate rollback actions:
  - Stop rollout and mark new images as paused.
  - Trigger deployment rollback command: redwoodctl rollback --target-release v2026.12.05 --scope runtime,control-plane
  - Restore metadata DB from preupgrade snapshot if schema changed and rollback requires restore.
- Postrollback review:
  - Open a postmortem, capture root cause, and schedule fix+retest before next attempt.

6.4 Emergency (fast) rollback for critical production incidents:
- If production outage > 5 minutes and no mitigation possible, execute emergency rollback playbook:
  - Run emergency command: redwoodctl emergency-rollback --release vX --force
  - Notify customers via status page and account contacts per SLA.
  - Engage incident response runbook and SRE engineers.

7) Troubleshooting and common failure modes

7.1 Common issues and remediation:
- Node GPU memory exhaustion:
  - Symptoms: OOM kills, GPU memory > 98% repeatedly.
  - Remediation: scale out node pool, offload high‑cost models to quantized variant, restart affected pods after draining.
- Model load failures:
  - Symptoms: model fails to initialize, repeated 502s on first token.
  - Remediation: verify artifact checksum, increase model load timeout, ensure NVMe mount/permissions.
- Network egress blocked (air‑gapped installs):
  - Symptoms: control plane unable to fetch updates, license activation fails.
  - Remediation: perform offline artifact import and manual license sync via redwoodctl --offline-activate.

8) Runbooks and playbooks (links and quick actions)
- Oncall playbook: /confluence/eng-private-deployments/private-deployments-runbook-2026-03-10
- Upgrade checklist: stored in repo releases/docs/upgrade-checklist.md and mirrored in the customer portal per deployment.
- Emergency rollback playbook: runbook ID PP-ER-2026 in PagerDuty runbooks.

9) Ownership, SLAs, and support model
- Ownership matrix:
  - Redwood product owner: packaging, signed artifacts, upgrade guidance.
  - Customer: underlying hardware, network, and physical security.
  - Redwood Professional Services: installation, initial sizing, and handover documentation (optional).
- Support tiers:
  - Standard: email support, best‑effort during business hours.
  - Enterprise: 24x7 SRE support, dedicated account engineering, SLA-backed response times.

10) Handoff and acceptance criteria for go‑live
- Acceptance checklist (must be completed and signed by customer):
  - All required ports verified and security groups applied.
  - Autoscaling and monitoring policies validated.
  - Snapshot and backup jobs configured and tested.
  - Performance validation tests meet agreed SLOs (p95 and error budget).
  - Documentation handover and runbook readout session completed.

Appendix A: Example validation test (curl based latency test)
- curl -X POST https://internal-redwood.example.com/v1/generate -H "Authorization: Bearer <token>" -d '{"model":"rwd-13b", "input":"Hello world"}'
- Run 1k requests with artillery or wrk and capture p50/p95/p99 for acceptance.
